days.title: Platform Components, Catalog Explorer Objects, Certified Tables, Metric Views, Lineage and Marketplace

concepts.heading: Platform Components and Who Uses Them
concepts.body: The Data Intelligence Platform is a lakehouse: open files in cloud object storage, Delta Lake as the default table format that adds ACID transactions, and Unity Catalog on top for governance. A workspace has a control plane that Databricks manages (web application, notebooks, SQL editor, job scheduling, workspace metadata) and a compute plane where data is processed; a serverless SQL warehouse runs in a compute plane inside the Databricks account, so the analyst configures no machines. Match the component to the person. Databricks SQL is the analyst's home: SQL editor, SQL warehouses, AI/BI Dashboards, alerts and Genie. Lakeflow is the data engineering side: Lakeflow Connect for ingestion, Lakeflow pipelines for declarative transformations and Lakeflow Jobs for orchestration. AI Functions let a SQL query call a hosted model, for example to classify review text. Lakebase is the managed Postgres database for low-latency transactional applications, which is a different job from analytical scans. One Unity Catalog metastore per region is shared by every workspace attached to it, so grants are defined once.

concepts.heading: Catalog Explorer: Objects and Names
concepts.body: Catalog Explorer is where an analyst browses what exists before writing a query. Objects are addressed as catalog.schema.object, so `sales.emea.orders` is the orders table in the emea schema of the sales catalog. A catalog is the top container, often per business unit or environment. A schema holds tables, views, volumes, functions and models. Tables govern rows; volumes govern files of any format such as PDFs, images or raw CSV, with paths like `/Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/file`. A view stores a query, and you can grant SELECT on the view alone so users see only the columns it exposes. A temporary view is different: it is registered in no schema, lives only in its session, and never appears in Catalog Explorer. For a table the explorer shows the schema with comments, sample data, owner and type (managed or external), permissions, lineage and insights. The word managed has layers: Unity Catalog governs every registered object, but a managed table also lets it choose the file location and lifecycle.

concepts.heading: Certified Tables, Metric Views and Lineage
concepts.body: Trust signals help analysts choose the right table. The system tag `system.certification_status` takes the value certified (met the organization's standards for accuracy, completeness and trust) or deprecated (outdated, do not use in new work). Applying it needs the ASSIGN permission on that governed tag, so only designated stewards can certify. A metric view solves a different problem: three dashboards defining revenue per customer differently. It separates measures, such as `sum(revenue) / count(distinct customer_id)`, from dimensions used to group and filter, defines them once in Unity Catalog, and lets dashboards, notebooks and Genie agents reuse the same definition. A standard view cannot do this because it fixes its aggregation at creation. Lineage is captured automatically for queries run on Databricks, down to the column level, and combined across workspaces on the metastore. Open a table's lineage graph for impact analysis before renaming a column. Referencing storage by path instead of by table name loses the column lineage.

concepts.heading: Databricks Marketplace
concepts.body: Databricks Marketplace is an open exchange where providers publish datasets, notebooks, AI models, apps and MCP servers, and consumers discover and request them. It is built on OpenSharing (Delta Sharing), so a dataset a consumer gets in a Unity Catalog workspace appears as a read-only shared catalog in the metastore and is queried like any table, joined with company tables, for example `provider_catalog.schema.table`. You can browse in the Open Marketplace without any workspace, but requesting access to a data product requires the Marketplace inside a workspace. Listings are either public or part of a private exchange that the provider shows only to member consumers, and access is either instant after agreeing to terms or subject to provider approval. Do not confuse it with Partner Connect, which creates trial accounts with technology partners and provisions the Databricks resources a partner tool needs. Marketplace is about obtaining data and assets; Partner Connect is about connecting tools.

examPoints: Databricks SQL, SQL warehouses and AI/BI Dashboards are the analyst-side components; Lakeflow is the engineering side; Lakebase serves transactional apps.
Names are catalog.schema.object; volumes hold files, tables hold rows, and a temporary view never appears in Catalog Explorer.
Marketplace data arrives as a read-only shared catalog; a metric view defines a measure once; lineage by name captures columns, by path it does not.

quiz.q: Three dashboards report different values for revenue per distinct customer, and the team wants a single governed definition that notebooks and Genie agents also reuse. What should an analyst create?
choices: A materialized view per dashboard, each refreshed on its own schedule to keep every figure fast and current
A standard view that fixes the aggregation and grouping once so that all consumers read the same rows
A metric view that defines the measure once, with dimensions for grouping and filtering
A certified tag on every dashboard dataset so that the three definitions are marked as officially approved
quiz.explain: A metric view separates measures from dimensions and is reused by dashboards, notebooks and Genie agents. A standard view locks in the aggregation at creation, and a certification tag is only a label, it does not unify the logic.

quiz.q: An analyst installs a free sample dataset from Databricks Marketplace in a Unity Catalog workspace and wants to add a derived column. What is true about the installed data?
choices: It is a read-only shared catalog, so derived columns go into the analyst's own table
It is copied into a managed table owned by the analyst, so columns can be added to it directly
It stays in the provider's workspace, so it can be queried only from the provider's own SQL warehouse
It is exposed as a volume of raw files that must first be loaded with Auto Loader before any SQL
quiz.explain: Marketplace data uses OpenSharing and lands as a read-only catalog. Enrich it with a query or CREATE TABLE AS SELECT into a schema the analyst can write to.

days.recap: The lakehouse combines open files, Delta tables and Unity Catalog. Analysts work in Databricks SQL, browse in Catalog Explorer, trust certified tables and metric views, check lineage before changes, and get external data from Marketplace as read-only shared catalogs.

days.title: Discovering Certified Data, Governed Tags, Lineage and SQL Data Cleaning

concepts.heading: Finding and Trusting a Dataset
concepts.body: Seeing that data exists and reading it are separate rights. BROWSE lets a user see an object's metadata (name, comments, lineage) in Catalog Explorer and in search without reading data. To query a table the user needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT, so an analyst can find a table in search and still get a permission error. Before choosing between lookalike tables, check three signals. The certification status tag shows whether stewards approved it as certified or flagged it deprecated. The Insights tab shows usage over the last 30 days, frequent queries, the dashboards and notebooks that read it and the tables usually joined to it. Comments on tables and columns also feed search, so a missing column description makes data harder to find. Catalog Explorer can suggest an AI-generated description as a starting point, which the owner should review. Deprecation is a label, not enforcement: a scheduled query that reads a deprecated table keeps running, and the table shows a restricted icon as the only warning.

concepts.heading: Governed Tags and Lineage
concepts.body: Tags are key-value labels on securable objects such as catalogs, schemas, tables and columns. Ungoverned tags are free form: anyone with APPLY TAG can use any key and value. Governed tags are account-level tags with a tag policy that defines the allowed values and who may apply them, so a `classification` tag accepts only `public`, `internal` or `pii` and analysts cannot invent others. Tags set on a catalog or schema are inherited by objects below, and tag search returns both direct and inherited matches. Tag data is stored as plain text and can replicate globally, so never put sensitive data in a tag name or value. Lineage follows the same permission model: a user needs BROWSE or SELECT on an object to see it, and anything else shows as a masked node. Column lineage shows which upstream columns produced `revenue`, which supports audit questions. Systems outside Unity Catalog, such as Salesforce upstream or Tableau downstream, appear only when registered as external metadata objects in external lineage.

concepts.heading: Cleaning NULLs and Invalid Values in SQL
concepts.body: Missing values are the first trap. Any arithmetic with NULL returns NULL, so `total - discount` drops out of sums when discount is missing. `COALESCE(discount, 0)` returns the first non-null argument and fills the gap. `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when the two are equal, which makes `revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0)` return NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error in ANSI mode. `x NOT IN (subquery)` returns no rows if the subquery produces even one NULL, so prefer NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out. In ANSI mode CAST raises an error on text such as `n/a`, while `try_cast(amount AS DOUBLE)` returns NULL and can be wrapped in COALESCE. Comparison is case sensitive and counts spaces, so `USA`, `usa` and `Usa ` group separately until you apply `lower(trim(country))`. Sentinel values like -999 for a failed reading should become NULL or be filtered out. A WHERE filter hides bad rows only for that query. The owner of a Delta table can run `DELETE FROM sensors WHERE temperature = -999` to remove them for everyone.

concepts.heading: Removing Duplicate Rows
concepts.body: DISTINCT collapses only rows that are completely identical, so it fails when repeated imports gave the same `user_id` different `updated_at` values. The reliable pattern is to number rows within each key and keep the newest: `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` assigns 1 to the latest row, and a filter on that number in an outer query or a QUALIFY clause keeps one row per user. The window function needs PARTITION BY to define the group and ORDER BY to define which row wins; without them the choice is arbitrary. GROUP BY with an aggregate such as `max(updated_at)` also finds the latest date but returns only the grouped columns unless you join back. After cleaning, decide where the result lives. A query or view applies the clean logic every time anyone reads it, which keeps the source untouched. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT stores a cleaned copy that can be certified and shared. DELETE changes the table itself, so use it only on tables you own and expect others to read the corrected rows.

examPoints: BROWSE shows metadata and lineage only; querying needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT. Deprecated tags warn but do not block queries.
Governed tags restrict allowed values and who applies them; tags are inherited and searchable; never store secrets in tags; masked lineage nodes mean no BROWSE.
COALESCE fills NULLs, NULLIF avoids divide-by-zero, try_cast turns bad text into NULL, NOT IN fails on NULLs, row_number deduplicates, DELETE removes rows for everyone.

quiz.q: An analyst can find a table in Catalog Explorer search and has BROWSE on its catalog, yet SELECT * on it fails. What explains this?
choices: The table is deprecated, and Unity Catalog blocks queries on every table carrying that certification status
The table is external, and external tables can be queried only by their original storage owner
Lineage for the table is masked, so the query planner refuses to read columns it cannot trace
BROWSE exposes metadata only, and reading data also needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT
quiz.explain: BROWSE separates discovery from access. Deprecation is a label, not enforcement, and external tables are governed like any other table.

quiz.q: A query `SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT payment_id FROM refunds)` returns 0 although many payments have no refund. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The refunds column holds NULLs, so the NOT IN predicate is never true for any payment row
The payments table needs DISTINCT because duplicate ids make count(*) collapse to zero in ANSI mode
The subquery must be wrapped in COALESCE or the optimizer reorders the join and drops all rows
The NOT IN operator is case sensitive and rejects ids that differ in leading or trailing spaces
quiz.explain: One NULL in the list makes the comparison unknown for every row. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out of the subquery.

days.recap: Discover with Catalog Explorer, trust certified assets and Insights, remember BROWSE is not SELECT. Governed tags control values, lineage respects permissions, and SQL cleaning relies on COALESCE, NULLIF, try_cast, NOT EXISTS and row_number.

days.title: Bringing Data into Databricks: Files, OpenSharing, Lakeflow Connect, Federation and Uploads

concepts.heading: Choosing an Ingestion Approach
concepts.body: The analyst question is which route fits the source and the freshness need. Files in S3 or a volume: explore with `read_files('s3://bucket/path/', format => 'json')`, a table-valued function that infers a schema so you can SELECT, filter and join without creating anything. When the data proves useful, copy it with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, because a view over read_files stores only the query and returns nothing once the bucket deletes the files. For new files that keep arriving, an analyst working in SQL can create a streaming table over a volume path that uses Auto Loader, which processes each file once, and refresh it on a schedule. SaaS applications and databases: Lakeflow Connect managed connectors create a connection, an ingestion pipeline and destination tables, and database connectors read only changes after the first full load. Another organization's live data: OpenSharing. Data that must stay where it is: query it in place with federation. Match the words in the scenario: incremental files, managed connector, live provider table, no copy.

concepts.heading: OpenSharing, Marketplace and Federation
concepts.body: OpenSharing (Delta Sharing, the older name) is an open protocol where a provider creates a share of tables and grants it to a recipient. A Databricks recipient mounts the share as a catalog and always sees the provider's current data without copying it. Tables, views and volumes in that catalog are read-only: SELECT, DESCRIBE and SHOW work, changes do not. To enrich shared data, query it and write the result into your own table. Marketplace delivers the same mechanism through listings. Lakehouse Federation is the opposite choice: when a policy forbids copying an operational database, or the need is occasional, create a connection and a foreign catalog and query the remote tables live over JDBC, read-only and governed by Unity Catalog. Federation puts load on the source database for every query, so for heavy repeated reads precompute the result in a materialized view. Ingestion tools such as Lakeflow Connect copy data in; sharing and federation read it where it lives. Pick by whether a copy is wanted or allowed.

concepts.heading: Uploading a Data File
concepts.body: For a file that lives on a laptop, the Workspace UI upload is the simplest route. Upload the file into a Unity Catalog volume with Catalog Explorer, then select the file and create a table from it, which produces a Unity Catalog managed table you can join in SQL. Uploading needs WRITE VOLUME on the volume, plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG; READ VOLUME alone lets a user list and read files but not upload, so an analyst who can read a volume may still see the upload rejected. Creating the table needs CREATE TABLE on the schema and a running SQL warehouse or compute to infer the schema. Choose the destination by content. Volumes govern non-tabular data such as images, PDFs, audio and raw CSV or JSON, with a path under `/Volumes/`, and they suit notebooks that process files without SQL. Tables suit rows you want to query, join and share. Files in a volume can also be read in place with read_files before deciding to load them. Keep large recurring feeds out of manual uploads and use an ingestion route instead.

examPoints: read_files explores files in place; CREATE TABLE AS SELECT keeps a stable copy; a view over read_files stores only the query.
OpenSharing shares live provider data as read-only catalogs; federation queries the source in place via connection plus foreign catalog; Lakeflow Connect copies from SaaS and databases.
UI upload goes to a volume first, then create a table; uploading needs WRITE VOLUME, not READ VOLUME.

quiz.q: A partner company that is also a Databricks customer offers a live product catalog table. An analyst wants it queryable in SQL, always current, without building a pipeline. What fits best?
choices: Export the table to CSV each night and load it with a scheduled file upload into a volume
Receive it through OpenSharing and query the shared catalog directly
Create a Lakeflow Connect connector to the partner and copy rows into a managed table
Build a view over read_files that points at the partner's storage bucket path directly
quiz.explain: OpenSharing exposes the provider's current data as a read-only catalog. Nightly exports are not live, and connectors and bucket views add copying or access the provider has not offered.

quiz.q: An analyst can read files in the volume main.raw.files but the Catalog Explorer upload of a CSV is rejected. Which privilege is missing?
choices: USE SCHEMA on the main catalog for the table that the file would later become
SELECT on the table that the file would later become after the upload
CREATE VOLUME on the schema that holds the raw volume and the file
WRITE VOLUME on the volume, together with USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG
quiz.explain: Reading uses READ VOLUME, while uploading, overwriting and deleting files needs WRITE VOLUME. The other privileges relate to tables or to creating volumes.

days.recap: Explore with read_files, copy with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, use Auto Loader through streaming tables for arriving files, Lakeflow Connect for SaaS and databases, OpenSharing for live provider data, federation to query in place, and volumes plus WRITE VOLUME for uploads.

days.title: Genie Code, the SQL Warehouse and Federated Joins

concepts.heading: Genie Code for Writing and Debugging SQL
concepts.body: Genie Code, formerly Databricks Assistant, is the AI coding and data assistant for developers and technical practitioners. It works in notebooks, the SQL editor, pipelines and dashboards, and gives three kinds of help: chat that writes code from a prompt, inline suggestions and autocomplete as you type, and error help after a failed run. For errors, Quick Fix handles basic problems such as a column typo with a one-click accept and run, while Diagnose Error reads the error and surrounding context for harder failures such as environment problems. It uses Unity Catalog metadata, meaning table and column names, descriptions and popular assets, so cryptic names like `c1` and `amt_x` give poor queries and adding comments improves future answers. It is governed by Unity Catalog: it can only touch data the signed-in user may access. Treat output as a draft. Review joins for wrong keys that duplicate rows and filters that drop valid rows before publishing. Do not confuse it with a Genie space (Genie Agent), which answers business questions over curated datasets.

concepts.heading: What the SQL Warehouse Does
concepts.body: Data lives in cloud storage, governance comes from Unity Catalog, and the SQL warehouse is the compute that runs the query. Warehouses are serverless, pro or classic; all include Photon, and serverless adds Intelligent Workload Management on Databricks-managed infrastructure. A stopped warehouse restarts automatically when a query, a scheduled job, a JDBC or ODBC connection or an opened dashboard needs it, provided the user has permission. Two permission layers apply: Unity Catalog privileges such as SELECT govern the data, while warehouse ACLs govern the compute. Can view lets a user see warehouses and query history but not run queries; Can use lets them run queries; Can manage administers it. So an analyst with SELECT but without Can use still cannot run anything. For sizing, cluster size mainly speeds up one heavy query (a spilling monthly report wants a larger size), while the minimum and maximum number of clusters handles concurrency (many analysts queuing at 9 a.m. want a higher maximum). Match the symptom: slow single query means size, waiting queries means cluster count.

concepts.heading: Joining a Delta Table with a Federated Source
concepts.body: Query federation lets an analyst query an external relational database such as PostgreSQL, SQL Server or Oracle in place, through JDBC, while Unity Catalog governs it. Setup has two steps in order: create a connection that stores the JDBC URL and credentials, then create a foreign catalog from that connection, which mirrors the remote database. Its tables then appear with three-level names such as `pg_fed.public.customers`, and an analyst joins them with a Delta table in one statement: `SELECT o.order_id, c.name FROM main.sales.orders o JOIN pg_fed.public.customers c ON o.cust_id = c.id`. The SQL you write is Databricks SQL, not the source dialect, and remote column types are mapped to Spark types, for example PostgreSQL `numeric` becomes a Spark decimal. Foreign catalogs are read-only and Catalog Explorer shows the connection a catalog uses. Each query runs against the live source, with filters pushed down where possible, so a dashboard that many people refresh can overload production. In that case create a materialized view on the federated result.

examPoints: Quick Fix handles simple errors, Diagnose Error handles harder ones; Genie Code respects Unity Catalog permissions and its SQL needs review.
Warehouse size helps one heavy query, cluster count helps concurrency; running queries needs Can use plus Unity Catalog SELECT.
Federation is connection first, foreign catalog second, read-only, queried with Databricks SQL; precompute heavy repeated federated reads.

quiz.q: On a pro SQL warehouse, many analysts run queries at 9 a.m. and some wait in a queue, although each query is fast once it starts. Which change addresses the symptom?
choices: Raise the cluster size one step so that every query receives more memory and cores
Switch the queries to the classic type so that Photon processes each of them separately
Increase the maximum cluster count so the warehouse scales out
Grant every analyst Can manage on the warehouse so their queries leave the queue sooner
quiz.explain: Queuing under many simultaneous queries is a concurrency problem, solved with more clusters. Size speeds up a single heavy query, and permissions do not change queueing.

quiz.q: An analyst runs an UPDATE statement on a table in a PostgreSQL foreign catalog and it fails. What explains this?
choices: The SQL warehouse must be switched to the classic type before any statement can modify federated tables
Foreign catalogs are read-only, so changes belong in the source database
The connection stores read credentials only, and a new connection must be created for each UPDATE statement
Genie Code must first translate the UPDATE statement into PostgreSQL syntax before it can run
quiz.explain: Lakehouse Federation gives governed read-only access, so modifications happen in the source system. Warehouse type and Genie Code do not change that, and a connection is not created per statement.

days.recap: Genie Code drafts and fixes SQL under the user's permissions. The SQL warehouse is the compute: size for a heavy query, clusters for concurrency, Can use plus SELECT to run. Federation needs a connection and a foreign catalog, is read-only and is queried with Databricks SQL.

days.title: Materialized Views, Streaming Tables, Dynamic Views and Managed versus External Tables

concepts.heading: Standard View, Dynamic View and Materialized View
concepts.body: Three similar-sounding objects solve different problems. A standard view is a saved query: every read runs the full query, so it is always current but pays full cost each time. A materialized view stores its result as a managed table, so reads are fast and the cost moves to refresh time; it suits expensive aggregations that feed dashboards and reports. A dynamic view is a regular view whose query uses user-dependent functions, `session_user()` for the email or `is_account_group_member()` for account groups (recommended for Unity Catalog data), so it applies row and column protection when read and stores no data. Example: `CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('auditors') THEN email ELSE 'REDACTED' END`. A dynamic view protects only what passes through it; anyone with SELECT on the base table still reads everything, so restrict the table itself. A materialized view can hide a sensitive column by leaving it out or by using MASK and ROW FILTER, so only a named group such as hr_team sees salary and others get NULL. The key contrast: a dynamic view applies logic at query time, a materialized view precomputes data.

concepts.heading: Creating and Refreshing Materialized Views
concepts.body: An analyst creates a materialized view in the SQL editor with CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW on a SQL warehouse. Databricks creates a serverless pipeline behind it to process the create and every refresh, so there is no compute to manage, and refresh status can be monitored in Catalog Explorer. Where possible Databricks computes changes incrementally rather than from scratch. Refresh can run on a cron schedule with SCHEDULE CRON, manually with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, or on trigger with TRIGGER ON UPDATE, which refreshes after upstream source data changes; Databricks recommends that for production when upstream loads land at unpredictable times, because a fixed cron may run too early or too late. Remember the tradeoff: results are as fresh as the last refresh, unlike a standard view. Materialized views are also useful over federated data, because a heavy remote aggregation runs once per refresh instead of once per dashboard viewer. The exam asks what you create for fast repeated reads: a precomputed object, not another plain view.

concepts.heading: Streaming Tables versus Materialized Views
concepts.body: A streaming table suits ingestion. It reads append-only sources such as files in a volume through Auto Loader, or message buses such as Kafka, and handles each input row only once, keeping state about what it has already read. A refresh evaluates only rows that arrived since the last update, so files landing after it ran show up in the next refresh, which explains why twenty late files are missing right after one. Because rows are not re-read, changing the query changes only new rows; a full refresh requeries everything. A materialized view recomputes its query result from its sources, so it can include aggregations, joins and corrections to old rows. Rule of thumb: ingest new rows once with a streaming table; transform, aggregate and serve results with a materialized view; use a dynamic view to filter or mask per user without storing a copy. Phrases in scenarios give it away: each row exactly once and append-only points to streaming tables, precomputed for dashboards points to materialized views, different users see different values points to dynamic views.

concepts.heading: Managed and External Tables
concepts.body: Managed and external tables look the same in queries and differ in who owns the files. A managed table lets Unity Catalog choose the storage location and control the file lifecycle, including automatic optimization such as file compaction; it is the default and recommended type for Delta Lake and Iceberg, which Databricks advises in most cases. Dropping a managed table permanently deletes its data files after a recovery period of 7 days by default. An external table registers files in a location you manage, using `CREATE TABLE name USING CSV OPTIONS (...) LOCATION '<path>'`; formats include DELTA, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, ORC and TEXT. Unity Catalog governs access, but dropping it leaves the files in place, which suits a folder that non-Databricks tools also write or read. Find out which type a table is with `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED`, whose Type row shows MANAGED or EXTERNAL. To load Parquet, CSV or JSON into a managed table, use `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT * FROM read_files(...)`. Choose external only when the files must stay where they are and be shared with other tools.

examPoints: Dynamic views filter or mask per user at query time and store nothing; materialized views store precomputed results; both leave the base table readable unless restricted.
Materialized views refresh by SCHEDULE CRON, manually, or TRIGGER ON UPDATE; streaming tables process each appended row once.
Managed: Unity Catalog owns files, dropped data is deleted after the recovery period; external: files stay after drop; check with DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED.

quiz.q: Auditors must see full customer emails while all other analysts see REDACTED, and the team wants no second copy of the data. What should they create?
choices: A materialized view that stores one masked copy of the emails for everyone with access
A dynamic view using is_account_group_member to return the email or REDACTED per user
A streaming table over the email column that is refreshed separately for each group
An external table over the same files with different column names for the auditor group
quiz.explain: A dynamic view applies user-based logic at query time and stores no data. Materialized views and streaming tables create stored results, and an external table adds nothing to masking.

quiz.q: A team has a curated sales table that only Databricks users read, and the analyst wants Databricks to handle file compaction and storage placement. Which table type fits?
choices: External table over a folder that the analyst manages and optimizes by hand
Temporary view registered in the session of each of the analysts using it
Unity Catalog managed table, which handles files and optimization
Foreign table in a federated catalog that mirrors an operational database
quiz.explain: Managed tables let Unity Catalog control storage and optimization, and they are the recommended default. External tables leave the file lifecycle to you.

days.recap: Pick the object by need: standard view for a saved query, dynamic view for per-user masking, materialized view for precomputed results, streaming table for append-only ingestion. Prefer managed tables; use external tables when files must stay put for other tools.

days.title: Aggregates, Joins, Set Operations, Sorting and Filtering

concepts.heading: Aggregates and NULLs
concepts.body: An aggregate collapses many rows into one value per group. `count(*)` counts every row, while `count(col)` counts only rows where col is not NULL, so `count(coupon_code) / count(*)` is the share of orders that used a coupon. `count(DISTINCT col)` counts unique non-NULL values exactly, which on billions of rows is expensive. When an estimate is enough, `approx_count_distinct(col)` uses the HyperLogLog++ algorithm and is accurate within about 5 percent by default; the optional second argument, `relativeSD`, tightens or loosens that bound. Other everyday aggregates are `sum`, `avg` (alias `mean`), `min`, `max`, `median`, `stddev` and `percentile`, and `FILTER (WHERE cond)` limits the rows a single aggregate sees: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'RETURNED')`. Each non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in GROUP BY, otherwise Databricks raises MISSING_AGGREGATION. For summary statistics of a whole column the analyst can combine those functions in one query, or, in a notebook, generate a data profile on a result to get summary statistics and visual insights without writing each aggregate.

concepts.heading: Joins and Fan-Out
concepts.body: A join combines columns from two tables on a condition. INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills right-side columns with NULL when nothing matches, which is the answer to a report such as all customers, including those who never ordered. RIGHT JOIN mirrors it, and FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. `LEFT SEMI JOIN` returns left rows that have a match but no right columns, and `LEFT ANTI JOIN` returns left rows that have no match, the most direct way to find customers without orders. CROSS JOIN returns every combination and is rarely wanted. The classic analyst error is fan-out: joining orders (one row per order) to order_items (many rows per order) repeats the order row once per item, so `sum(orders.total)` counts each order several times and revenue is overstated. The fix is to aggregate the many-side to one row per key in a subquery or CTE first, then join. The EXPLODING_JOIN performance insight flags joins that produce far more rows than they read.

concepts.heading: Set Operations
concepts.body: Set operators stack the results of two queries instead of widening them. `UNION ALL` keeps every row from both queries, duplicates included, and is the cheapest because no comparison is needed. `UNION` (the same as `UNION DISTINCT`, the default) removes duplicate rows and so costs an extra deduplication step. `INTERSECT` returns rows present in both queries, and `EXCEPT` returns rows of the first query that are not in the second, which is handy for comparing two snapshots of a table. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types, otherwise Databricks raises NUM_COLUMNS_MISMATCH or INCOMPATIBLE_COLUMN_TYPE. Columns are matched by position, not by name: `SELECT id, name, city` stacked with `SELECT id, city, name` runs without error but puts cities under the name column. Always list columns in the same order. Choose a join when the goal is more columns per entity, and a set operation when the goal is more rows with the same shape, such as combining sales_2025 and sales_2026.

concepts.heading: Sorting and Filtering
concepts.body: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so a condition on `sum(sales)` belongs in HAVING, placed after GROUP BY; putting an aggregate in WHERE fails. `QUALIFY` filters on window function results, for example keeping the newest row per customer with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated DESC) = 1`, without a wrapping subquery. ORDER BY sorts the final result, ascending by default; add DESC for newest first. By default NULLs sort first in ascending order and last in descending order, and `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` overrides that. `LIMIT n` returns n rows, so `ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 10` returns the ten most recent orders; without ORDER BY the rows returned are not guaranteed to be the same each time. A comparison with NULL is never true, so `WHERE manager_id = NULL` returns nothing; use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`, and `IS DISTINCT FROM` when NULL should count as an ordinary value.

examPoints: count(*) counts all rows, count(col) skips NULLs, and approx_count_distinct trades a few percent of accuracy for speed on very large tables.
A join that fans out repeats the one-side values, so aggregate the many-side first; LEFT ANTI JOIN finds rows with no match, FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.
UNION ALL keeps duplicates, UNION removes them, and set operations match columns by position, so column order must be the same in both queries; conditions on aggregates go in HAVING.

quiz.q: An analyst needs the distinct visitor count over several billion web events for a trend chart on a dashboard. A result within a few percent of the exact value is acceptable, and the query must finish quickly. Which expression fits?
choices: count(visitor_id), which skips NULLs and returns the number of unique visitors in the column
approx_count_distinct(visitor_id), a HyperLogLog++ estimate with about 5 percent default accuracy
count(DISTINCT visitor_id), which always scans and deduplicates exactly and is the faster choice on large data
sum(DISTINCT visitor_id), which adds each unique value and returns how many visitors exist
quiz.explain: approx_count_distinct trades a small, bounded error for much lower cost on large inputs. count(col) counts all non-NULL rows including repeats, count(DISTINCT) is exact but costlier, and sum adds values instead of counting them.

quiz.q: A query UNIONs `SELECT id, name, city FROM a` with `SELECT id, city, name FROM b`. It runs, but the name column now contains cities for the second table. What is the cause, and how is it fixed?
choices: UNION matches columns by name only when the types are equal, so the second query needs explicit CAST calls
UNION ALL must replace UNION, because plain UNION sorts the columns of each side alphabetically
A join on id is required, because set operations cannot combine two tables with the same column names
Set operations match columns by position, so both SELECTs must list columns in the same order
quiz.explain: Set operators pair columns by ordinal position and need compatible types; they never look at names. Swapping to UNION ALL only changes duplicate handling, and a join widens rows instead of stacking them.

days.recap: Aggregates: count(*) counts rows, count(col) skips NULLs, approx_count_distinct estimates. Joins: LEFT keeps the left side, ANTI finds non-matches, and a one-to-many join fans out sums. Set operations stack rows by position (UNION ALL keeps duplicates). WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups, QUALIFY filters windows, and NULL needs IS NULL.

days.title: Time Travel and Delta History for Audit and Comparison (T4.9, T5.3)

concepts.heading: Every Write Is a Version
concepts.body: A Delta table records each operation that changes it, such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE or OPTIMIZE, as a numbered version in its transaction log. Time travel lets an analyst query the table as it was at one of those versions without changing the current data. Use `SELECT * FROM prices VERSION AS OF 12` for a version number or `SELECT * FROM prices TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-11-01'` for a point in time. The shorthand `prices@v12` also names a version. Typical analyst uses are re-creating a report as it looked last week, finding what a faulty job changed, and getting a stable snapshot. Because the old state is read-only, it is safe to experiment. To compare two states, pair it with a set operator: `SELECT * FROM prices EXCEPT SELECT * FROM prices VERSION AS OF 12` returns rows that exist now but did not at version 12. `RESTORE TABLE prices TO VERSION AS OF 12` is different: it actually rolls the table back, needs the MODIFY privilege, and is a data change, not a query.

concepts.heading: How Far Back Time Travel Reaches
concepts.body: Time travel needs both the log entry and the data files of the old version. Two table properties control this. `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` (default 7 days) decides how long VACUUM keeps data files that the current version no longer uses. `delta.logRetentionDuration` (default 30 days) decides how long history entries are kept. Because the shorter one wins in practice, the documentation advises relying on only the past 7 days for time travel unless both properties have been raised. Once VACUUM has removed the files of a version, a query on that version fails and a RESTORE to it is no longer possible. Predictive optimization runs VACUUM automatically but still honors the retention window, and keeping more history raises storage cost. This matters for reporting: if finance must reproduce a month-end figure for two years, time travel on the source table is not a reliable archive. Save the result with `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` as its own snapshot table and report from that.

concepts.heading: DESCRIBE HISTORY as an Audit Trail
concepts.body: `DESCRIBE HISTORY finance.ledger` returns one row per write, newest first, with the version, timestamp, user, operation and more; `LIMIT 1` returns just the last operation. Catalog Explorer shows the same data on the History tab. So the question who last changed this table, when, and with what kind of operation is answered by the user, timestamp and operation columns. Two columns carry detail. `operationParameters` holds how the operation was run, for example a MERGE predicate, or for OPTIMIZE rows whether `auto` is true (automatic compaction after writes) or false (a command from a user or job). `operationMetrics` holds counts, such as rows inserted, updated and deleted by a MERGE, which lets an analyst confirm that a nightly job touched the expected number of rows. History retention follows `logRetentionDuration`, 30 days by default. The CONCURRENT_WRITE performance insight tells the analyst to read this history to find overlapping writes and then stagger the jobs.

concepts.heading: Validating and Comparing Historical Results
concepts.body: A common audit question is why a number changed between two reports. The method has three steps. First run DESCRIBE HISTORY to find the versions or timestamps that match each report and the operation between them. Second, read both states with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF. Third, compare them: EXCEPT in both directions lists added or removed rows, while a join on the business key shows changed values side by side, for example `FROM sales_summary cur JOIN sales_summary VERSION AS OF 40 old USING (month) WHERE cur.revenue <> old.revenue`. Aggregates on both states, such as `sum(revenue)`, confirm that a change in a total is explained by the rows found. Pair the result with the history row's user and operation to say who changed it and how. Remember the limits: if the old files were vacuumed, the version cannot be queried, so audit work on tables that matter should be done inside the retention window or from saved snapshots.

examPoints: VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF query an old state read-only; RESTORE actually rolls the table back and needs MODIFY.

Time travel reaches only as far as the data files survive VACUUM: deletedFileRetentionDuration defaults to 7 days, logRetentionDuration to 30 days; reproducible long-term figures need a snapshot table.
DESCRIBE HISTORY shows user, timestamp and operation per write; operationParameters shows how it ran, operationMetrics shows row counts.

quiz.q: Finance must reproduce each month-end revenue figure for two years. The source Delta table uses default retention settings and VACUUM runs regularly. What should the analyst do?
choices: Save each month-end result as its own table with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT and report from that snapshot
Rely on TIMESTAMP AS OF against the source table, because history entries are kept for two years by default
Run DESCRIBE HISTORY each month and store the output, since it can rebuild old rows
Run RESTORE on the source table every month to freeze that month's data in place
quiz.explain: With default retention the data files of old versions are removed by VACUUM, so time travel cannot serve a two-year requirement. A snapshot table stores the figures independently. DESCRIBE HISTORY lists operations, not row data, and RESTORE would roll back live data.

quiz.q: An auditor asks which user last changed the finance.ledger Delta table, when, and with what kind of operation. What returns this?
choices: SELECT * FROM finance.ledger VERSION AS OF 0, which lists the writers of the table's first load
DESCRIBE DETAIL finance.ledger, which returns the full list of users who ever wrote to the table
DESCRIBE HISTORY finance.ledger LIMIT 1, giving the operation, user and time of the last write
SHOW TBLPROPERTIES finance.ledger, which stores the last editor as a property of the table
quiz.explain: DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per write with version, timestamp, user and operation, newest first. A time travel query returns table data, not audit columns, and table properties do not record the last writer.

days.recap: Time travel queries old versions read-only (VERSION AS OF, TIMESTAMP AS OF); RESTORE changes the table. It works only while files survive VACUUM (7 days of file retention, 30 days of log by default), so keep snapshot tables for long-term figures. DESCRIBE HISTORY gives user, time, operation, parameters and metrics, and EXCEPT or a key join compares states.

days.title: Photon, Query Profile and Fixing a Query (T5.1, T5.2, T5.6)

concepts.heading: What Photon Does
concepts.body: Photon is the Databricks-native vectorized query engine written in C++. The optimizer still plans the query, but for supported operations Photon executes it in columnar batches instead of the JVM-based Spark engine, which speeds up SQL, DataFrame API calls, ETL batch jobs and stateless streaming without any code change. It is on by default for all SQL warehouses, so an analyst neither switches it on nor rewrites queries. The gain is largest for long-running queries over large data, such as scans with joins and aggregations on a big fact table; queries that already finish in about two seconds gain little because planning and scheduling dominate. If a query contains an operation Photon does not support, execution falls back to the standard Spark engine for that part, and the rest may still run in Photon. The query completes and returns correct results, just more slowly, and the COVERAGE_PHOTON insight flags it. Stateful streaming is not supported by Photon. The analyst decision is therefore to expect help on heavy read queries and not to expect it on tiny lookups.

concepts.heading: Reading Query Insights and the Profile
concepts.body: Open a slow query from Query History to see the details panel: wall-clock duration with a breakdown of scheduling, optimization and execution; aggregated task time, the combined time across all cores of all nodes, which can exceed wall-clock time because tasks run in parallel; and I/O metrics. See longest operators opens the Top operators panel, which lists the most expensive steps so costly ones stand out without reading the whole plan graph. See query profile opens the detailed graph of operators. Query performance insights appear in the same panel, ranked by estimated effect, and in the Performance insights tab. Each insight has a recommendation. WIDE_PROJECTION means the query reads all columns, so select only needed ones. EXPLODING_JOIN means a join produces far more rows than it reads. DATA_FILE_SIZE means many small files, so run OPTIMIZE or enable predictive optimization. DATA_SPILL means memory ran out, and EXCESSIVE_QUEUE_TIME means the warehouse needs more clusters. Insights labeled Accelerated, such as SHORT_QUERY_PRIORITIZATION, report something Databricks already did and need no action.

concepts.heading: Acting on Insights
concepts.body: When an insight is actionable, Optimize opens Genie Code. For insights that need a query change, Genie Code rewrites the query and shows the changes for the analyst's approval; for table or compute changes it only summarizes the recommended actions in plain language and does not apply them. Match the fix to its owner: query text problems belong to the analyst, while layout and warehouse sizing may need a table owner or an admin. A profile can be shared by downloading it as JSON, which a colleague imports in query history with Import query profile (JSON), useful when the colleague lacks permission on the query. For a table, MANUAL_DATA_LAYOUT suggests converting an externally managed, manually optimized table to a managed table with predictive optimization and automatic clustering. The general sequence is: find the slow query in history, read the top operators and insights, change one thing, and rerun with caching disabled in the editor so that timing is honest. Insights are hints, so confirm that the result still returns the same rows.

concepts.heading: Fixing a Query That Gives the Wrong Result
concepts.body: Fix tasks usually come down to a small set of recognizable mistakes. A non-aggregated column missing from GROUP BY raises MISSING_AGGREGATION; add it to GROUP BY or wrap it in an aggregate. An aggregate in WHERE fails because WHERE runs before grouping; move the condition to HAVING. `WHERE manager_id = NULL` returns no rows because comparing with NULL is never true; use `IS NULL`. A SUM that is too high after a join is fan-out: aggregate the many-side to one row per key in a subquery first, then join. A UNION that places values in the wrong columns needs the same column order in both queries. A LEFT JOIN with a WHERE condition on a right-side column silently becomes an inner join, because the NULL rows are filtered out; move the condition into the ON clause. An INNER JOIN where unmatched rows were expected should become a LEFT JOIN. Read the error text first: Databricks error names such as MISSING_AGGREGATION and NUM_COLUMNS_MISMATCH point at the clause to change.

examPoints: Photon is the default engine on SQL warehouses, helps most on long scans, joins and aggregations, and falls back to Spark for unsupported operations without failing the query.

Top operators shows the costliest steps; aggregated task time is summed across cores and can exceed wall-clock time; Optimize in Genie Code rewrites query-level fixes for approval and only summarizes table or compute changes.
Know the fixes: MISSING_AGGREGATION needs GROUP BY, aggregate conditions use HAVING, NULL needs IS NULL, join fan-out needs pre-aggregation.

quiz.q: A dashboard query that used to finish in seconds now takes minutes. From query history, an analyst wants to see which individual steps consumed the most time without reading the whole plan graph. Which part helps?
choices: The aggregated task time field, which shows the total number of cores used by the query
The wall-clock duration field, which splits the run into one line per SQL clause and operator
The Top operators panel, which lists the longest-running operators
The Query source link, which opens the notebook or dashboard that holds the query text
quiz.explain: Top operators ranks the most expensive operators. Aggregated task time is one summed number, wall-clock duration shows only scheduling, optimization and execution phases, and Query source navigates to where the query lives.

quiz.q: An analyst runs SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region and gets a MISSING_AGGREGATION error. The report needs one row per region and product. What is the fix?
choices: Change GROUP BY region to GROUP BY region, product so every non-aggregated column is grouped
Wrap region in SUM so the engine can group the rows without listing it
Move the SUM expression into a WHERE clause so the groups are filtered before they form
Replace GROUP BY with ORDER BY region, product so that each combination is sorted into one row
quiz.explain: Every selected column that is not inside an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY. SUM on a text column is invalid, WHERE cannot hold an aggregate, and ORDER BY sorts rows but never groups them.

days.recap: Photon: default on SQL warehouses, no code changes, falls back to Spark for unsupported parts, best on long large scans. Query history gives wall-clock duration, aggregated task time, Top operators and insights with recommendations; Optimize in Genie Code rewrites queries and summarizes table or compute advice. Fix wrong queries by recognizing the pattern: GROUP BY columns, HAVING, IS NULL, fan-out, column order.

days.title: Query History, Caching, Predictive Optimization and Automatic Liquid Clustering (T5.4, T5.5)

concepts.heading: Query History for Development
concepts.body: Query History in the sidebar lists the SQL and Python queries that ran on SQL warehouses and, when serverless compute is enabled, on serverless compute for notebooks and jobs. Filters narrow the list by user, date range, compute, duration, query status, statement type, statement ID and query tags. That answers practical questions: which query did I run last week that joined these tables, and which queries on this warehouse took longer than a minute. A query is tagged Queued, Running, Finished, Failed or Cancelled, and a running query can be cancelled from its details. Opening a row shows the full statement, user and compute, the metrics, the query profile and performance insights. Re-using a past statement saves development time, because the analyst copies the working version instead of rewriting it. History is also the starting point for tuning: sort by duration, open the slowest, and read its top operators and insights. Query source links back to the dashboard, notebook or saved query that issued it.

concepts.heading: Caches on a SQL Warehouse
concepts.body: Databricks SQL has several caches that explain why a rerun is faster. The result cache stores the result of a query per cluster: an identical query on unchanged tables returns almost instantly. Its local part lives in memory for the cluster's lifetime and is lost when the warehouse stops or restarts; the remote result cache is serverless-only and survives a stop because the results are persisted as workspace system data. The disk cache keeps data files read from storage on local SSDs, so later scans are faster, and it is invalidated when it detects that the underlying files changed. The disk cache and the local result cache are cleared on stop, so the first heavy query after an overnight auto stop is slow, while later runs are fast. The Databricks SQL UI cache shows each user the latest result in the editor, and it does not apply to AI/BI dashboards, which have their own caching behavior. To time a rewrite fairly, run `SET use_cached_result = false` in the SQL editor session so results are recomputed.

concepts.heading: Predictive Optimization
concepts.body: Predictive optimization is a managed service for Unity Catalog managed tables (not external tables). Databricks identifies the tables that would benefit and queues `OPTIMIZE` (file compaction and clustering), `VACUUM` (removing unreferenced files) and `ANALYZE` (statistics for better plans), and it collects statistics at write time. It runs on serverless compute, so the analyst does not size a cluster or schedule maintenance. It can be set for the account, a catalog, a schema or a table, and lower levels inherit the account value unless they override it. Turning it off at the account level does not turn it off for a catalog or schema that explicitly enabled it. Changing the setting on a table needs the table owner or the MANAGE privilege, not just SELECT and MODIFY. Observability comes from the system table `system.storage.predictive_optimization_operations_history`, which records what ran, costs and impact, and from the History tab in Catalog Explorer. VACUUM still respects the retention window of `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration`, which matters for time travel.

concepts.heading: Automatic Liquid Clustering
concepts.body: Liquid clustering organizes data by clustering keys so queries that filter on those columns skip files, and Databricks recommends it over partitioning and Z-ordering. Choosing keys by hand is hard when filters change over time. With `CLUSTER BY AUTO`, Databricks selects and changes the keys from how the table is actually queried, using predictive optimization for key selection and clustering; it applies to Unity Catalog managed tables and runs asynchronously. A key change happens only when the predicted data-skipping savings outweigh the cost of reclustering, so if filters move from store_id to product_category, the keys may follow, though not instantly. Keys may be absent on a table that is small, already well laid out or rarely queried. A partitioned managed table can be converted with `ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY AUTO`. In query profiles, AUTO_LIQUID_CLUSTERING marks a query that read less data thanks to it, and MANUAL_DATA_LAYOUT recommends converting a manually optimized external table to a managed table with predictive optimization and automatic clustering.

examPoints: Query History filters by user, date range, compute, duration, status, statement type and tags; result cache and disk cache are cleared when a warehouse stops, and SET use_cached_result = false gives honest timings.

Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE only where useful, on Unity Catalog managed tables; its setting needs the table owner or MANAGE, and the account-level off switch does not override explicit catalog or schema enablement.
CLUSTER BY AUTO lets Databricks choose and change clustering keys from query patterns, only when savings outweigh reclustering cost; it needs a managed table.

quiz.q: A pro SQL warehouse is stopped every night by auto stop. Each morning the first run of a heavy dashboard query is slow, while reruns later in the day are fast. Why?
choices: Photon is disabled by auto stop and must be switched on again by an admin each morning
Predictive optimization deletes the table statistics overnight and recollects them on the first query
The Databricks SQL UI cache expires at midnight and recomputes the query on every dashboard viewer's first open
The local result cache and the disk cache are cleared when the warehouse stops, so they must be repopulated
quiz.explain: Result and disk caches live on the warehouse and are lost on stop or restart, so the first run reads from storage. Photon stays on for SQL warehouses, predictive optimization does not drop statistics, and the UI cache does not apply to AI/BI dashboards.

quiz.q: A managed table was partitioned by event_date, but analysts now filter mostly by customer_id or region, and the patterns keep shifting. The team wants the layout to adapt without manual tuning. What fits?
choices: Add a second partition column for customer_id and rely on predictive optimization to merge partitions
Convert to liquid clustering with CLUSTER BY AUTO, so keys follow query patterns
Run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY customer_id once a week from a scheduled job
Convert the table to an external table so queries read files directly without a layout step
quiz.explain: CLUSTER BY AUTO uses predictive optimization to select and adjust clustering keys for managed tables as filters change. More partitions worsen over-partitioning, Z-order keys are fixed and manual, and external tables get no automatic layout.

days.recap: Query History filters and opens the profile of past queries. Result cache (identical query, unchanged data) and disk cache (files on SSD) are lost when a warehouse stops; the remote result cache is serverless-only. Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE on managed tables, controlled by the owner or MANAGE. CLUSTER BY AUTO picks clustering keys from query patterns when the gain justifies the cost.

days.title: Building AI/BI Dashboards: Datasets, Pages and Widgets, Plus Notebook and SQL Editor Charts

concepts.heading: Datasets Feed Widgets
concepts.body: An AI/BI dashboard has two tabs. The Data tab holds datasets and the Canvas tab holds pages with widgets: visualizations, filters, text and images. A dataset is defined once, from a Unity Catalog table, view or metric view, or from your own SQL query, and any number of widgets on any page can read it. A table or view starts as a default `SELECT *` query that you can narrow. A dataset is a security decision as well as a layout one: viewers can reach all data in a dataset even when no chart shows a column, so Databricks recommends listing only the columns you need and adding a `WHERE` clause for the rows you need. A salary column that sits in the dataset is exposed even if every chart ignores it. Datasets travel with the dashboard when it is shared, imported or exported, so there is no separate query object to keep in step.

concepts.heading: Pages, Drafts and Publishing
concepts.body: A dashboard can hold several pages, which turns it into a multi-page report. A page can be cloned within the dashboard, and the datasets stay the same. A page copied into another draft dashboard brings its datasets as new, independent copies. Hide from published dashboard keeps a scratch page visible to authors only, which is safer than deleting it because deleting a page removes its widgets. New dashboards open as drafts; edits autosave but do not flow to a published version, and a draft can be shared only with users inside the workspace, who use their own credentials. Publishing creates a snapshot that stays unchanged until the next publish, so managers keep seeing the old numbers while you experiment. Discard changes restores the draft to the last published version. Opening a dashboard that was published before shows the published version first.

concepts.heading: Where Filtering and Aggregation Run
concepts.body: Dashboards avoid asking the warehouse again whenever they can. For small datasets, filtering and aggregation that come from filters or chart settings run in the browser after the first load, so they do not show up in query history. For large datasets they run on the backend, wrapped around the dataset query, and they appear in query history. This explains a common surprise: a filter on a small dataset reacts instantly, while the same filter on a very large dataset triggers a query. Query parameters always change the SQL itself, so they always run on the warehouse. The practical analyst rule is to shape the dataset first (needed columns, needed rows, pre-aggregated when the chart only needs totals), then let widgets slice it. Heavy transformations belong in the dataset query or in a view, not in many separate widgets.

concepts.heading: Charts in Notebooks and the SQL Editor
concepts.body: Outside dashboards you build a chart under a result: click + above the result and choose Visualization, then pick a type and fields. For bar, line, area, pie, heatmap and histogram charts you can aggregate in the visualization editor (sum, average, count and so on) instead of rewriting the query, and the aggregation covers the whole result, not only the rows the results table displays. A filter on the visualization also filters the results table, and the other way around, without changing the SQL. Clicking a legend entry hides or shows a series and double-clicking isolates one. A chart under a SQL cell offers Add to dashboard, which lists dashboards or creates a new one; charts from other languages and data profiles can only go to a notebook dashboard. Use the SQL editor or notebook for exploration and a dashboard for sharing a stable view.

examPoints: A question about viewers seeing columns no chart shows is testing that the whole dataset is visible to viewers, so the dataset query lists only needed columns and rows instead of `SELECT *`.
A question about hiding a working page, throwing away experiments, or what viewers see after edits is testing Hide from published dashboard, Discard changes, and the draft versus published snapshot.

A question about switching sum to average on a chart in the SQL editor is testing aggregation in the visualization editor, and one about sending a chart to a dashboard is testing that Add to dashboard exists only for SQL cells.

quiz.q: An analyst built a bar chart under a Python cell in a notebook and wants colleagues to see it on a shared dashboard. What is the limitation she should expect?
choices: The chart can be added to a dashboard only when the notebook is attached to a serverless SQL warehouse instead of a general cluster
Only SQL cells offer Add to dashboard; other languages stay in a notebook dashboard
The chart is converted automatically, but its aggregation settings are dropped and must be rebuilt on the dashboard canvas
The chart is shared through Add to dashboard, which lists every dashboard the analyst may edit, whatever the cell language is
quiz.explain: Add to dashboard is offered for SQL cells. Charts and data profiles from other languages stay in a notebook dashboard, so the analyst would define a SQL dataset on an AI/BI dashboard and rebuild the chart there.

quiz.q: An author edits the draft of an already published dashboard, changing a filter and two charts. Managers open the dashboard the next morning and still see the old charts. What explains this?
choices: Draft edits sync to viewers only after the next scheduled refresh runs all the dataset queries again
Viewers always see the draft version when the author has CAN EDIT access, so the managers lack a needed permission
Autosave only covers widget layout, so changes to filters must be exported and imported to appear for viewers
Published dashboards are snapshots; draft edits wait for the next publish
quiz.explain: Draft changes autosave but do not sync with the published version. Viewers see the snapshot from the last publish, which is why authors can experiment safely and use Discard changes to go back.

days.recap: Define datasets once on the Data tab, select only the columns and rows viewers may see, and reuse them across pages. Drafts autosave privately and viewers see only the last published snapshot. Small datasets filter in the browser, large ones on the warehouse, and parameters always rerun the query. In the SQL editor and notebooks, aggregate in the visualization editor, and use Add to dashboard only from SQL cells.

days.title: Dashboard Parameters, Filters and Cross-Filtering, and Choosing the Right Visualization Type

concepts.heading: Parameters Change the Query
concepts.body: A parameter is a named marker such as `:start_date` in the SQL text; the value is substituted when the query runs. In the SQL editor you set the parameter's type (text, number, date and so on) in a widget, so colleagues type a value instead of editing SQL. In a dashboard dataset, parameters connect to filter widgets, or to a visualization as a static value set by the author so that several widgets on one dataset show different views. Always type the default value into the field under the parameter name and run the query, which saves the default. Because the value goes into the SQL, parameters filter before aggregation or inside a subquery, and they always rerun the query on the warehouse. Two patterns matter for the exam. Multiple selection requires `array_contains(:region, region)`, and enabling multiple selections is needed or the function raises an error. A range uses `:date_param.min` and `:date_param.max` with `BETWEEN`. Add `OR :param IS NULL` so that All returns every row.

concepts.heading: Field Filters or Parameters
concepts.body: A field filter narrows the dataset result by a column and needs no parameter in the SQL. Field filters are usually the more efficient choice: for small datasets they run in the browser without rerunning the query, and for large ones the filter is added to the query that the warehouse runs. They also support cascading, so choosing a region narrows the choices offered in a city filter. Use a parameter when the value must reach the query before a join, aggregation or subquery, or when you build a drop-down from a separate `SELECT DISTINCT` dataset and bind both the field and the parameter to the same filter widget. Filter scope has three levels. Global filters apply across all pages for widgets that share a dataset; page-level filters apply to one page; widget-level filters are fixed by the author and cannot be changed by viewers, so they give one chart a permanent slice. Date pickers, ranges, single and multiple value lists, text entry and range sliders are the available filter types, with some limited to fields.

concepts.heading: Cross-Filtering and Ignored Filters
concepts.body: Cross-filtering lets a viewer click a bar, a slice or a point in one chart to filter the other widgets built on the same dataset. The active filter bar at the top of the dashboard shows every global filter, page filter and cross-filter that is not set to All, so a viewer can see why numbers changed. When one chart must stay fixed while the rest of the dashboard reacts, the author sets that widget to ignore selected filters or cross-filter selections. That is different from a widget-level filter: an ignored filter exempts a widget from viewer choices, while a widget-level filter applies a permanent author-chosen condition. Filter values can also be set in the published dashboard URL, which is useful for bookmarked views. Cross-filtering depends on the shared dataset, so two charts on unrelated datasets will not respond to each other even if their column names match.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Visualization
concepts.body: Start from the question, then choose the type. A trend over time is a line chart, or an area chart when you also show how groups add up. Comparing categories is a bar chart. Shares of a total fit a pie, which is not meant for time series. The spread of one numeric column is a histogram, where the number of bins sets the grain, and a box chart compares quartiles across groups. Two numeric measures are a scatter chart, and a third measure as marker size makes it a bubble chart. Drop-off through ordered stages is a funnel with a step and a value column. A running total built from positive and negative steps, such as opening to closing balance, is a waterfall. A single headline KPI with a comparison value is a counter. A heatmap shows a number as colour across two categories and a pivot or table is for exact values. Stick to the built-in types for these needs.

examPoints: A question about letting viewers pick several values and also an All option is testing a multi-select parameter written with `array_contains` and an `OR :param IS NULL` branch, and a date range with `.min` and `.max`.

A question about a small dataset, a fixed chart slice, or one selection across pages is testing field filter versus parameter, widget-level versus page-level versus global filter, and ignored filters.

A question that describes the business need in words (trend, shares, drop-off, distribution, opening to closing balance, one KPI) is testing the type: line, pie, funnel, histogram, waterfall, counter.

quiz.q: A dashboard dataset has a few thousand rows, and viewers only need to narrow the chart by customer segment. A teammate proposes adding a query parameter for the segment. What is usually the better fit?
choices: A field filter on the segment column, which small datasets apply in the browser without rerunning the query
A page of copies of each chart with the segment value typed into the dataset query by hand
A parameter bound to a text entry widget, so that every selection reruns the warehouse query before aggregation
A global parameter on the dataset that is hidden from viewers and set only by the author at publish time
quiz.explain: Field filters are usually the better fit: on small data they apply in the browser, on large data the filter is added to the query, and they cascade. Parameters are for values that must reach the SQL before a join, aggregation or subquery.

quiz.q: A finance analyst must explain how the opening cash balance of a quarter became the closing balance, with each inflow and each outflow as its own step. Which visualization fits?
choices: A stacked area chart with one series per inflow and outflow, plotted by week across the quarter
A funnel chart where every step is a cash category and the width shows the amount remaining
A waterfall chart where each category adds to or subtracts from the running total
A pie chart of the absolute value of each cash category, so executives see the share of each movement
quiz.explain: A waterfall shows the cumulative effect of sequential positive and negative values, which is exactly an opening to closing bridge. A funnel is for drop-off between ordered stages and a pie shows shares of a whole.

days.recap: Parameters rewrite the SQL (typed marker, default value, array_contains for multi-select, .min/.max for ranges, OR IS NULL for All) and always rerun the query. Field filters suit small data and cascade. Scope is global, page, or fixed widget-level, and widgets can ignore filters. Match the chart to the question: line trend, bar compare, pie share, histogram spread, scatter/bubble relation, funnel drop-off, waterfall bridge, counter KPI.

days.title: Sharing and Embedding Dashboards, Scheduled Refresh and SQL Alerts

concepts.heading: Publish Settings and Access Levels
concepts.body: Sharing starts with Publish, where you choose whose data permissions the queries use. Share data permissions (the default) runs queries as the publisher, so viewers need no access to the underlying data, which fits managers who must not touch the tables, but it can expose data they have not been granted. Individual data permissions runs queries as each viewer, so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per person; compute still comes from the publisher. Access levels are CAN VIEW and CAN RUN to look and interact, CAN EDIT to edit and publish, and CAN MANAGE to change permissions and delete. A registered account member without workspace access is capped at CAN RUN, even if the dialog shows more. Share with a user, a group, or everyone in the account with Anyone in my account can view. Dashboards also inherit the permissions of the folder that holds them. A draft always uses the viewer's own data permissions, whatever the published setting is.

concepts.heading: Embedding a Dashboard
concepts.body: Only published dashboards can be embedded. Basic embedding generates iframe code from the Share dialog; viewers sign in with their Databricks account, only users granted access can see it, and a workspace admin must first define the allowed embedding surfaces. When the viewers are customers or partners who have no Databricks account, use embedding for external users, in which your application authenticates with a service principal and an OAuth token, and the user never signs in to Databricks. Databricks recommends publishing such a dashboard with individual data permissions and giving the service principal only the access it needs, because with shared data permissions the publisher's access determines the data. If an iframe stays blank, the documented fix is to enable third-party cookies in the browser; also confirm the dashboard is published, the viewer has access and the admin allowed the surface. Embedded viewers can refresh the dashboard on demand.

concepts.heading: Scheduled Refresh and Subscriptions
concepts.body: A schedule runs all the dataset SQL at a chosen frequency, start time and time zone, and fills the query result cache so the first viewer after the run opens the dashboard quickly. With shared data permissions the cache is shared by all viewers, so one early run helps the Monday crowd. The dashboard cache is best effort and can serve results up to a day old, and a pipeline finishing does not refresh it, so a schedule is the reliable way. With individual data permissions each viewer keeps a personal cache; a viewer chooses Refresh data for me to warm it without notifications, or Refresh data for me & email to also get a snapshot, or Inactive for me to opt out. A start time anchors the cadence: every 4 hours from 15:10 runs at 15:10, 19:10 and 23:10 and resets to 15:10 the next day. Subscriptions send PDF or image snapshots to email, Slack or Microsoft Teams, with optional CSV, TSV or Excel data.

concepts.heading: Databricks SQL Alerts
concepts.body: An alert runs a query on a schedule and notifies people when a condition on the result is met. In the alert editor you write the query, pick a SQL warehouse, set a schedule, choose the condition and the notification recipients. The condition checks the first value of a column or an aggregate such as sum or average, compares it with a static value using an operator, and Test condition previews it. Current alerts own their query: you cannot pick an existing saved query, so paste the SQL in. Each evaluation ends as OK, TRIGGERED or ERROR, and a recovered metric returns to OK. By default you are notified when the alert triggers. A notification frequency repeats the message until the alert returns to OK, Notify on OK sends a message when the alert returns to OK, and Empty result state decides the status when the query returns no rows. Recipients can be users or notification destinations that a workspace admin defined, such as a webhook.

examPoints: A question about viewers with no access to the tables is testing Share data permissions, while one about per-person row filters or masks is testing Individual data permissions.

A question about customers outside the account seeing a dashboard in a portal is testing embedding for external users with a service principal and OAuth, and a blank iframe is testing third-party cookies first, then publish state, access and allowed surfaces.

A question about slow first loads or fresh personal results is testing a schedule that fills the cache and Refresh data for me; one about repeated or recovery messages is testing notification frequency and Notify on OK.

quiz.q: A support lead receives one alert email when the open ticket count passes a limit, but she wants the email repeated until the count is back under the limit. Where is this configured?
choices: In the dashboard schedule dialog, by adding a second subscriber who receives the failure snapshot as well
In the advanced settings, through Empty result state, which keeps the alert triggered until the query returns rows again
In the alert condition, by lowering the threshold so the alert keeps evaluating as triggered each time
In the alert's Notifications, with a repeat frequency until OK
quiz.explain: The notification frequency repeats messages until the alert returns to OK. Notify on OK is the separate setting that sends a message at recovery, and Empty result state only chooses the status for a query with no rows.

quiz.q: A company wants customers, who are not members of its Databricks account, to see a dashboard inside the company's own web portal. Which approach fits?
choices: Embedding for external users, where the application authenticates with a service principal and OAuth
Basic embedding, after adding every customer to the Databricks account as a registered member who signs in
A shareable link with Anyone in my account can view, pasted into the portal page as a normal hyperlink
A scheduled subscription that emails each customer a PDF of the dashboard after every scheduled refresh run
quiz.explain: Embedding for external users lets an application show a dashboard to people without Databricks accounts by authenticating as a service principal. Basic embedding and account-level links require each viewer to be a known account member.

days.recap: Publish chooses whose data permissions run the queries: shared for viewers without data access, individual for row filters and masks per person. CAN RUN/VIEW use, CAN EDIT edit and publish, CAN MANAGE permissions and delete. Embed only published dashboards: basic with sign-in, external users with a service principal. A schedule fills the cache (shared or personal) and drives subscriptions. Alerts own their query; use frequency to repeat and Notify on OK for recovery.

days.title: AI/BI Genie Agents: Purpose, Components and Creating a Genie Agent
